newsitem.title: USA: Has insurance industry heeded warning?.
newsitem.headline: Has insurance industry heeded warning?.

text.p: Four years after Hurricane Andrew ravaged southern Florida -- and the U.S. insurance industry -- Hurricane Fran approached the South Carolina coast Thursday, posing the worst threat to a U.S. city since Andrew landed.

As hurricane forecasters closely monitored the massive storm's progress toward Charleston others wondered not only how the homes and businesses along its path would fare, but also how any damage would affect the companies that insure them.
"I'm not sure that you ever avoid chaos in that kind of (Andrew-like) hurricane," said Gary Ransom, an analyst at Conning & Co. in Hartford.
After Andrew cut its swath south of Miami in August 1992 and then hit Lousiana and caused some $18 billion in insured losses, insurers were blindsided, confessing they had never imagined such a loss.

"I think some of the companies may have lost track of where exactly their insureds were living," said John O'Connell, professor of international insurance at the Thunderbird School Management in Phoenix, Ariz. "No one really expected one that large to come through."
Andrew sent a handful of small insurers into insolvency. Even the largest insurers, such as State Farm Insurance Co. and Allstate Insurance Co. were hit hard.

For consumers, Andrew made homeowners policies much more expensive, with higher deductibles. It has also been very difficult for some to obtain, as companies left Florida or cut back operations there.
State Farm has raised premiums in Florida by an average of about 60 percent and Allstate by about 50 percent since Andrew, according to the Florida Department of Insurance.

"The ones that were hit hard by Andrew originally, which include all the big personal lines writers, most of them have been avoiding writing any additional business in those areas," Ransom said. "Allstate in particular has devised a solution to considerably reduce their own exposure over time."

Charleston, S. C., the largest city that appeared at risk from Fran on Thursday, has about 500,000 people in its metropolitan area. The city was slammed seven years ago by Hurricane Hugo, a Category 4 storm that passed just to its north, causing more than $4 billion in insured losses.

Industry experts said Fran likely would not lead to insurance chaos similar to that of Andrew, even if its effects were to be similar to Hugo's. That's because companies have cut back their exposure in hurricane-prone areas and spread out the financial risk from a severe loss despite a series of disasters -- notably California's Northridge earthquake -- since Andrew.

"They are in worse shape financially, but they have more tools now to work with," said Barry Schweig, a professor of finance at Creighton University in Omaha, Neb., who has studied the insurance market extensively.
Experts said any hurricane's landfall will make insurance more troublesome for consumers, with policies more difficult to get and prices rising even higher.
"The stocks would probably go up if there was a hurricane," Conning said. "If the hurricane happens, then you would assume that you would have the opportunity for rates to go up even more."

State Farm and Allstate are the biggest insurers in South Carolina, according to the Insurance Information Institute. State Farm has 29.11 percent of the state's market share, with $103.2 million in direct written premiums, and Allstate has 15.45 percent of the market, with $54.8 million in such premiums.

In North Carolina, State Farm is also the largest, with 17.61 percent of the market and $104.5 million in direct written premiums. Nationwide Mutual Insurance Co. is No. 2 in the state, with 15.49 percent and $92.4 million in direct written premiums, the institute said.

But as Fran edged toward the Carolinas, industry experts said their real concern was not another Andrew, but some kind of mega-storm worse than Andrew, Hugo or Fran, especially one that could strike a coastal area home to millions of people.
"There's still considerable concern," said Suzanne Douglass, a senior vice president at Alexander & Alexander Inc. in New York.

"Every time a storm comes, it just brings to mind that people have overbuilt in exposed areas, and its very difficult for the industry to get its arms around what the maximum loss that they could incur from any one event."
